lesson.title: From a Kentucky Cabin to the White House: Abraham Lincoln's Rise
lesson.summary: Abraham Lincoln rose from a self-educated frontier lawyer to the presidency on the strength of his opposition to slavery's expansion, and he led the Union through the Civil War until his assassination in April 1865.
lesson.body:
Abraham Lincoln was born on February 12, 1809, in a log cabin in Hardin County, Kentucky, to a farming family with little money and almost no access to formal schooling. His family moved first to Indiana and later to Illinois as he grew up, and Lincoln later estimated his total time in a classroom at less than a year; he taught himself law largely by reading borrowed books while working odd jobs, including splitting rails and running a small store, before earning admission to the Illinois bar in 1836. He built a successful law practice in Springfield, Illinois, and served in the Illinois state legislature and then a single term in the United States House of Representatives from 1847 to 1849, where he was a fairly minor figure known mainly for opposing the Mexican-American War.

Lincoln's national reputation was made not by winning an election but by losing one. In 1858 he challenged incumbent Senator Stephen Douglas in a series of seven debates held across Illinois, arguing that slavery's expansion into the territories had to be stopped even though the Constitution protected it where it already existed. Douglas won the Senate seat, but newspapers across the country printed transcripts of the debates, and Lincoln emerged as one of the Republican Party's clearest and most persuasive voices on the central issue of the day. That reputation carried him to the Republican nomination in 1860 and then to the presidency, where he took office on March 4, 1861, already facing seven seceded states and the loss of most federal property across the Deep South.

As president, Lincoln proved willing to use powers that no previous president had claimed on nearly the same scale, suspending habeas corpus in parts of the country, expanding the army without prior congressional authorization in the war's opening weeks, and eventually issuing the Emancipation Proclamation as a war measure under his authority as commander in chief. He was a shrewd political manager who worked to hold together a fractious coalition of Republicans, war Democrats, and border state Unionists, and he cycled through several generals, including George McClellan, before finding in Ulysses S. Grant a commander willing to fight the sustained, costly campaigns Lincoln believed were necessary to end the war.

Lincoln won reelection in 1864, helped substantially by Union battlefield victories that year, and delivered a second inaugural address in March 1865 calling for reconciliation with malice toward none. He did not live to see that reconciliation attempted. On the evening of April 14, 1865, just five days after Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox, Lincoln was shot by John Wilkes Booth while attending a play at Ford's Theatre in Washington, and he died early the next morning, April 15, 1865. His death left the enormous work of Reconstruction, and the fate of nearly four million newly freed people, to a country that had just lost the president who had steered it through the war.
